items.stem: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.2 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.05. Determine, with a reason, whether A and B are (a) mutually exclusive; (b) independent.
items.markingKey: (a) R1 P(A ∩ B) = 0.05 ≠ 0, so not mutually exclusive. (b) P(A)P(B) = 0.1 (M1); R1 not equal to P(A ∩ B), so not independent.

items.stem: A fair 12-sided die, numbered 1 to 12, is rolled. The experiment is repeated 200 times and "the score is at least 2" occurs 193 times. Compare the relative frequency with the theoretical probability and explain why they differ.
items.markingKey: A1 relative frequency 193/200 = 0.965; A1 theoretical 11/12 = 0.917; R1 random variation – they are expected to be close for large n but not equal.

items.stem: A fair 8-sided die and a fair 6-sided die are rolled and the product of the two scores is recorded. Draw a sample space diagram and find P(product > 25).
items.markingKey: Grid of 48 outcomes (M1); count 9 (A1); 3/16 (A1).

items.stem: The probability that a customer is a member is 0.4. If a customer is a member, the probability that the customer buys a coffee is 0.7; otherwise it is 0.2. Find the probability that the customer buys a coffee.

A bag contains 15 yellow, 5 white, 2 green counters. One counter is taken at random. The experiment is carried out 60 times (with replacement where relevant). Find the expected number of times that it is yellow.
A box contains 4 red and 5 green sweets. Two are taken at random without replacement. Draw a tree diagram and find the probability that the two sweets are different colours.
items.markingKey: Tree with correct second-stage probabilities (M1 A1); 4/9 × 5/8 + 5/9 × 4/8 (M1) = 5/9 (A1).

items.stem: The probability that a seed is treated is 0.5. If a seed is treated, the probability that the seed germinates is 0.6; otherwise it is 0.3. Find the probability that the seed germinates.

Records show that the probability that a flight from Mumbai departs on time is 0.6. The experiment is carried out 150 times (with replacement where relevant). Find the expected number of times that a given flight departs on time.

In a group of 45 students, 31 own a cat, 10 own a dog and 7 do neither. (a) Draw a Venn diagram. (b) Find the probability that a student chosen at random does exactly one of the two. (c) Find P(B | A).

The probability that a student revises is 0.8. If a student revises, the probability that the student passes is 0.9; if a student does not revise, it is 0.5. (a) Draw a tree diagram. (b) Find the probability that the student passes. (c) Given that the student passes, find the probability that a student revises. (d) Determine whether the events "a student revises" and "the student passes" are independent, giving a reason.

At a school fair a game costs 5 NZD to play. A player wins a prize of 4 NZD (and does not get the stake back) with probability 1/3. (a) Find the expected number of winners in 500 games. (b) Find the expected profit for the organisers over 500 games. (c) Find the prize that would make the game fair. (d) Comment on the use of relative frequency to check the probability 1/3.
items.markingKey: (a) 500 × 1/3 (M1) = 167 (A1). (b) income 2500 − prizes 667 (M1) = 1830 (A1). (c) prize × 1/3 = 5 (M1) ⇒ 15.0 (A1). (d) R1 a large number of trials is needed for the relative frequency to be a good estimate.

items.stem: A fair 4-sided die and a fair 4-sided die are rolled and the product of the two scores is recorded. (a) Draw a sample space diagram. (b) Find P(product > 9). (c) Find the expected product. (d) In 50 games a player wins whenever the product exceeds 9; find the expected number of wins.

The probability that a student revises is 0.5. If a student revises, the probability that the student passes is 0.4; if a student does not revise, it is 0.6. (a) Draw a tree diagram. (b) Find the probability that the student passes. (c) Given that the student passes, find the probability that a student revises. (d) Determine whether the events "a student revises" and "the student passes" are independent, giving a reason.
Which term matches this description: "A grid listing all equally likely outcomes of two combined experiments, e.g. two dice"?
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of sample space diagram.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "combined events formula"?
options: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
The set U of all possible outcomes of an experiment
A ∩ B, outcomes in both A and B
A grid listing all equally likely outcomes of two combined experiments, e.g. two dice
items.answer: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
items.markingKey: A. "combined events formula" is P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

items.stem: Which value cannot be a probability?

In a group of 47 students, 29 like coffee, 23 like tea and 10 do neither. Nia says the probability a randomly chosen student does at least one activity is (29 + 23)/47. Explain the error and find the correct probability.
items.markingKey: R1 the 15 students in both groups are counted twice; M1 (29 + 23 − 15)/47; A1 37/47.

items.stem: P(A) = 0.8, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. Determine, with a reason, whether A and B are (a) mutually exclusive; (b) independent.
items.markingKey: (a) R1 P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 ≠ 0, so not mutually exclusive. (b) P(A)P(B) = 0.32 (M1); R1 not equal to P(A ∩ B), so not independent.

items.stem: A bag contains 7 white, 13 green, 6 black counters. One counter is taken at random. The experiment is repeated 60 times and "it is white" occurs 20 times. Compare the relative frequency with the theoretical probability and explain why they differ.
items.markingKey: A1 relative frequency 20/60 = 0.333; A1 theoretical 7/26 = 0.269; R1 random variation – they are expected to be close for large n but not equal.

items.stem: A box contains 9 red and 4 green sweets. Two are taken at random without replacement. Tomás calculates P(both red) = (9/13)². Explain why this is incorrect and find the correct probability.
items.markingKey: R1 without replacement the second probability is 8/12, not 9/13; M1 9/13 × 8/12; A1 6/13.

items.stem: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.05. Determine, with a reason, whether A and B are (a) mutually exclusive; (b) independent.
items.markingKey: (a) R1 P(A ∩ B) = 0.05 ≠ 0, so not mutually exclusive. (b) P(A)P(B) = 0.09 (M1); R1 not equal to P(A ∩ B), so not independent.

items.stem: A bag contains 3 black, 6 green, 12 blue counters. One counter is taken at random. The experiment is repeated 120 times and "it is black" occurs 25 times. Compare the relative frequency with the theoretical probability and explain why they differ.
items.markingKey: A1 relative frequency 25/120 = 0.208; A1 theoretical 1/7 = 0.143; R1 random variation – they are expected to be close for large n but not equal.

items.stem: A box contains 5 red and 6 green sweets. Two are taken at random without replacement. Draw a tree diagram and find the probability that the two sweets are different colours.
items.markingKey: Tree with correct second-stage probabilities (M1 A1); 5/11 × 6/10 + 6/11 × 5/10 (M1) = 6/11 (A1).

items.stem: The probability that a seed is treated is 0.5. If a seed is treated, the probability that the seed germinates is 0.9; otherwise it is 0.7. Find the probability that the seed germinates.
A fair 12-sided die, numbered 1 to 12, is rolled. The experiment is carried out 200 times (with replacement where relevant). Find the expected number of times that the score is at least 6.
A fair 4-sided die and a fair 4-sided die are rolled and the sum of the two scores is recorded. Draw a sample space diagram and find P(sum > 5).
items.markingKey: Grid of 16 outcomes (M1); count 6 (A1); 3/8 (A1).

items.stem: The probability that a seed is treated is 0.2. If a seed is treated, the probability that the seed germinates is 0.6; otherwise it is 0.7. Find the probability that the seed germinates.

Records show that the probability that a flight from Nairobi departs on time is 0.3. The experiment is carried out 360 times (with replacement where relevant). Find the expected number of times that a given flight departs on time.
A box contains 7 red and 3 green sweets. Two are taken at random without replacement. Draw a tree diagram and find the probability that the two sweets are different colours.
items.markingKey: Tree with correct second-stage probabilities (M1 A1); 7/10 × 3/9 + 3/10 × 7/9 (M1) = 7/15 (A1).

items.stem: The probability that the alarm goes off is 0.3. If the alarm goes off, the probability that Kenji is on time is 0.7; if the alarm does not go off, it is 0.6. (a) Draw a tree diagram. (b) Find the probability that Kenji is on time. (c) Given that Kenji is on time, find the probability that the alarm goes off. (d) Determine whether the events "the alarm goes off" and "Kenji is on time" are independent, giving a reason.

At a school fair a game costs 2 EUR to play. A player wins a prize of 21 EUR (and does not get the stake back) with probability 1/36. (a) Find the expected number of winners in 100 games. (b) Find the expected profit for the organisers over 100 games. (c) Find the prize that would make the game fair. (d) Comment on the use of relative frequency to check the probability 1/36.
items.markingKey: (a) 100 × 1/36 (M1) = 2.78 (A1). (b) income 200 − prizes 58.3 (M1) = 142 (A1). (c) prize × 1/36 = 2 (M1) ⇒ 72.0 (A1). (d) R1 a large number of trials is needed for the relative frequency to be a good estimate.

items.stem: A box contains 7 black and 5 white pens. Two are taken at random without replacement. (a) Draw a tree diagram. (b) Find the probability that both are the same colour. (c) Given that both are the same colour, find the probability that both are black. (d) Find the probability of different colours if the first one is replaced before the second is taken, and explain why it differs.
items.markingKey: (a) A2. (b) 7·6 + 5·4 over 12·11 (M1) = 31/66 (A1). (c) P(both black)/P(same) (M1) = 21/31 (A1). (d) 2 × 7/12 × 5/12 = 35/72 (A1); R1 with replacement the events are independent.

items.stem: A screening test for a genetic condition affects 5% of a population. The test is positive for 90% of people with the condition and negative for 90% of people without it. (a) Draw a tree diagram. (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen person tests positive. (c) Find the probability that a person who tests positive has the condition. (d) Comment on your answer to (c) in context.
items.markingKey: (a) A2. (b) 0.05 × 0.9 + 0.95 × 0.1 (M1) = 0.140 (A1). (c) 0.0450/0.140 (M1) = 0.321 (A1). (d) R1 most positive results are false positives because the condition is rare – a second test is needed.
